title: Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
authors_full: Zongyi Li, Nikola Kovachki, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, Burigede Liu, Kaushik Bhattacharya, Andrew Stuart, Anima Anandkumar
affiliations: No explicit affiliation block printed; inferred from printed emails: Zongyi Li, Nikola Kovachki, Burigede Liu, Kaushik Bhattacharya, Andrew Stuart, Anima Anandkumar at Caltech (California Institute of Technology, USA, @caltech.edu); Kamyar Azizzadenesheli at Purdue University, USA (@purdue.edu)
venue: ICLR (International Conference on Learning Representations; 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2021')
verification: full-text verified (all 16 pages read: main text pp.1-9, references pp.10-12, Appendix A pp.13-16)
subdomain: turbulent 2-d Navier-Stokes (vorticity form) with zero-shot super-resolution; 1-d Burgers; 2-d Darcy subsurface flow; Bayesian inverse problem for initial vorticity
industry_context: No named deployment; motivated by molecular dynamics, microelectronics, turbulent flows and inverse-design loops ('when designing materials such as airfoils, one needs to solve the associated inverse problem where thousands of evaluations of the forward model are needed', p.1). Funded by Army Research Laboratory (Cooperative Agreement W911NF-12-0022 and W911NF-12-2-0022); sponsors include Beyond Limits, Raytheon, Microsoft, Google, Adobe (Acknowledgements, p.10)
problem_class: operator (learns the parametric family map G-dagger: a -> u for an entire distribution of PDE instances; also used as fast forward surrogate in a Bayesian inverse problem)
physics_enforced_exact: No physics is enforced in the loss (purely data-driven operator learning). The governing equations defining the learned operators, in the paper's own form: 1-d Burgers: du/dt u(x,t) + d/dx(u^2(x,t)/2) = nu d^2u/dx^2 u(x,t), x in (0,1), t in (0,1], periodic BCs, u(x,0)=u0(x), nu=0.1 (Eq. 6); 2-d steady Darcy flow: -div(a(x) grad u(x)) = f(x), x in (0,1)^2, u(x)=0 on boundary (second order, linear, elliptic) (Eq. 7); 2-d Navier-Stokes for a viscous, incompressible fluid in vorticity form on the unit torus: d/dt w(x,t) + u(x,t).grad w(x,t) = nu Laplacian w(x,t) + f(x), div u = 0, x in (0,1)^2, t in (0,T] (Eq. 8)
pde_type: multiple (Burgers: nonlinear viscous/parabolic; Darcy: linear elliptic; Navier-Stokes: viscous incompressible parabolic in vorticity form)
dimensionality: 1-d Burgers (space+time, maps u0 to u(.,1)); 2-d Darcy; 2-d Navier-Stokes (2-d space + time; FNO-3D variant treats time as a third convolution dimension, 64x64x20 -> 256x256x80)
nonlinearity: mixed: Burgers and Navier-Stokes contain nonlinear advection terms (u^2/2 and u.grad w, turbulent regime nu=1e-4/1e-5); Darcy PDE is linear but the coefficient-to-solution operator G-dagger is nonlinear (paper: 'although the PDE is linear, the operator G-dagger is not')
bcs_ic_handled: Burgers: periodic boundary conditions on (0,1); initial condition u(x,0)=u0(x) is the operator input. Darcy: homogeneous Dirichlet u=0 on boundary of (0,1)^2; forcing kept fixed f(x)=1. Navier-Stokes: periodic BCs on the unit torus; initial vorticity w(x,0)=w0(x) is the input; fixed forcing f=0.1(sin(2pi(x1+x2))+cos(2pi(x1+x2))). Conditions are embedded in the training data (solutions of classical solvers), never imposed at training time; non-periodic boundaries (Darcy, NS time domain) are absorbed implicitly by the linear transform W (bias term), Section 5.5 p.9
enforcement_mechanism: operator - no soft-penalty/hard-constraint/variational mechanism exists; physics enters only through the training data, making FNO the canonical operator-learning counterpoint to PINN-style residual enforcement
enforcement_details: No autodiff PDE residual is formed. The map G-dagger: A -> U is learned purely from pointwise input-output pairs {a_j, u_j} generated by classical solvers: Burgers solved with split-step Fourier (heat part exact in Fourier space, nonlinear part advanced by forward Euler) on a 2^13=8192 mesh; Darcy by second-order finite differences on a 421x421 grid; Navier-Stokes via stream-function pseudo-spectral with Crank-Nicolson (dt=1e-4, de-aliased) on 256x256, downsampled to 64x64. PDE knowledge is instead used in the design choices: vorticity formulation, fixed forcing, and Fourier-truncated kernel
network_architecture: Fourier Neural Operator: input a lifted by pointwise P to v0 = P(a(x)) in R^dv; T=4 Fourier layers v_{t+1}(x) = sigma(W v_t(x) + F^-1(R_phi . (F v_t))(x)) where R is a learnable weight tensor applied on the k_max truncated Fourier modes and W is a local linear transform; output u(x) = Q v_T(x) with pointwise Q. d_v=64, k_max,j=16 for 1-d Burgers; d_v=32, k_max,j=12 for 2-d problems. Variants: FNO-2D (2D convolutions + RNN in time, 411,517 params) and FNO-3D (convolves directly in space-time, Table 1 prints 0.6,558,537 params). Built on the neural operator framework of Li et al. 2020b (Graph Kernel Network) by replacing the kernel integral operator with a convolution parameterized directly in Fourier space
input_representation: pointwise evaluations (grid values) of the input function a(x) on discretization D_j = {x_1,...,x_n}: initial condition u0 for Burgers/NS; diffusion coefficient field a for Darcy; FNO-3D ingests 3-d space-time tensors of initial time steps
output_representation: solution function evaluated on the same grid: u(.,1) for Burgers; pressure field u for Darcy; vorticity trajectory w up to time T for Navier-Stokes (FNO-3D maps initial time steps directly to the full trajectory, 3D functions to 3D functions)
loss_terms: min_theta E_{a~mu}[C(G(a,theta), G-dagger(a))] (Section 2, Eq. context p.3); in practice the empirical surrogate over the N training pairs {a_j, u_j}; a single supervised data term - no PDE-residual, boundary, or regularization terms are stated (relative L2 error is the reported quantity in all tables)
loss_weighting: fixed (single data term; no weighting scheme discussed)
sampling_strategy: not applicable - no collocation sampling: supervised operator learning on uniform grids; N=1000 training / 200 testing pairs for Burgers and Darcy; N=1000 or N=10000 for Navier-Stokes; lower-resolution grids downsampled from higher-resolution data (p.6)
optimizer_schedule: Adam, 500 epochs, initial learning rate 0.001 halved every 100 epochs (Section 5, p.6)
training_compute: single Nvidia V100 GPU with 16GB memory; time per epoch: FNO-3D 38.99s, FNO-2D 127.80s, U-Net 48.67s, TF-Net 47.21s, ResNet 78.47s (Table 1, p.8)
transfer_or_pretraining: zero-shot super-resolution / discretization transfer: trained on 64x64x20 (nu=1e-4, N=10000) and directly evaluated on 256x256x80 without any higher-resolution data (Section 5.4, Figure 1); parameters are resolution-invariant because they are learned in Fourier space
uq_method: Bayesian inverse problem: function-space Markov chain Monte Carlo (Cotter et al. 2013) with FNO as surrogate forward operator; posterior of the initial vorticity of Navier-Stokes given sparse noisy observations at time T=30; 25,000 posterior samples (5,000 burn-in) requiring 30,000 forward-operator evaluations (Section 5.5). No intrinsic UQ of the network itself
data_regime: dense simulation data (physics-only in the sense of no experimental measurements): Burgers N=1000 train/200 test generated on 2^13=8192 mesh; Darcy 421x421 FD solutions (s in {85,141,211,421} downsampled); Navier-Stokes N=1000 or N=10000 pairs generated on 256x256 grid downsampled to 64x64, dt=1e-4, solution recorded every t=1
datasets_used: 1-d Burgers equation (nu=0.1, u0 ~ N(0, 625(-Delta+25I)^-2)); 2-d Darcy flow on unit box (a ~ psi#N(0,(-Delta+9I)^-2), f=1); 2-d Navier-Stokes in vorticity form on unit torus (w0 ~ N(0, 7^{3/2}(-Delta+49I)^-2.5); nu = 1e-3 (T=50), 1e-4 (T=30), 1e-5 (T=20))
baselines_compared: Burgers/Darcy: NN (pointwise feedforward), GCN, FCN (fully convolutional), PCANN (PCA+autoencoder), RBM (classical Reduced Basis Method, Darcy only), GNO (graph neural operator), LNO (low-rank kernel operator), MGNO (multipole graph neural operator). Navier-Stokes (64x64): FNO-2D, U-Net, TF-Net, ResNet. Traditional solvers (FEM/FDM) and Neural-FEM not compared since the goal is efficient operator approximation (Section 5, p.6)
evaluation_metrics: relative L2 error (vs. resolution and vs. method); parameter count; time per epoch; inference time per forward evaluation; MCMC wall-clock time; qualitative posterior-mean comparison for the Bayesian inverse problem
key_quantitative_results: Burgers: FNO rel. L2 = 0.0149 (s=256) to 0.0139 (s=8192), best of all 8 methods at every resolution and invariant to resolution (Table 3). Darcy: FNO rel. L2 = 0.0108/0.0109/0.0109/0.0098 (s=85/141/211/421) - 'nearly one order of magnitude lower relative error compared to any benchmarks' (p.8, Table 4). Navier-Stokes at 64x64 (Table 1): FNO-3D rel. L2 = 0.0086 (nu=1e-3, T=50, N=1000), 0.1918 (nu=1e-4, N=1000), 0.0820 (nu=1e-4, N=10000), 0.1893 (nu=1e-5, N=1000); FNO-2D: 0.0128/0.1559/0.0834/0.1556. Contribution claims (p.3): error rates 30% lower on Burgers, 60% lower on Darcy, 30% lower on Navier-Stokes (nu=1e-4) vs. existing deep learning methods at 64x64; <1% error over the entire time series with nu=1e-3 and 8% with nu=1e-4. Inference 0.005s vs 2.2s on a 256x256 grid; Bayesian inverse MCMC 2.5 minutes (FNO) vs over 18 hours (traditional solver)
speedup_claims: 'It is up to three orders of magnitude faster compared to traditional PDE solvers' (abstract, p.1); inference 0.005s (FNO) vs 2.2s (pseudo-spectral, tuned to largest non-blow-up time-step) on 256x256 Navier-Stokes (p.3, Section 5.5); Bayesian inverse MCMC: 2.5 minutes with FNO vs over 18 hours with the traditional solver; even accounting for offline data generation + training of 12 hours, FNO is still faster (p.9); learning-based methods in general 'can be orders of magnitude faster than the conventional solvers' (p.1)
ablations: (1) FNO-2D (2D conv + RNN in time) vs FNO-3D (space-time convolution): 3-d method more expressive and easier to train, best with sufficient data; FNO-2D lowest error when data insufficient (Table 1). (2) Resolution sweep 256-8192 (Burgers) and 85-421 (Darcy) showing FNO error is resolution-invariant while FCN/NN/GCN error grows. (3) Data-amount ablation on NS nu=1e-4: rel. L2 0.1918 (N=1000) -> 0.0820 (N=10000). (4) Parameterization of R: linear parameterization similar to direct parameterization; neural-network parameterization worse ('likely due to the discrete structure of the space Z^d', p.6). (5) Spectral analysis (Sec 5.5, App A.2, Figures 4-5): truncating a nu=1e-3 solution at 20 Fourier modes yields ~2% error while FNO reaches <=1% with only k_max,j=12; spectrum of NS data decays as k^{-5/3}
stated_limitations: Section 6 (p.9): 'Requirements on Data' - to learn Navier-Stokes with nu=1e-4 needs N=10000 solver-generated training pairs; 'for more challenging PDEs, generating a few training samples can be already very expensive'; future direction is combining neural operators with numerical solvers to alleviate data requirements. 'Recurrent structure' - parameter sharing across layers was not imposed in experiments. Section 2 (p.3): existence of minimizers in the infinite-dimensional setting 'remains a challenging open problem'. Section 4 (p.6): the chosen mode set Z_kmax 'is not the canonical choice for the low frequency modes'; a uniform discretization is required for FFT. Section 5.5 (p.9): output of Eq. 4 has at most k_max Fourier modes per channel (FNO can only approximate functions up to k_max modes; high-frequency recovery relies on activations and the decoder Q)
failure_modes: graph-based neural operators 'do not converge' in the turbulent Navier-Stokes regime (contribution bullet, p.3); standard CNN methods (FCN/NN/GCN) have error that grows with resolution (p.6, Figure 3a); with insufficient training data (NS nu=1e-4 N=1000, nu=1e-5 N=1000) 'all methods have >15% error' (p.8); neural-network parameterization of the Fourier weights underperforms the direct tensor (p.6); traditional Fourier methods fail on non-periodic boundaries (mooted for FNO via the W term, p.9)
reproducibility: No code or data URL is printed in the PDF. Fully specified training configuration: Adam, 500 epochs, lr 0.001 halved every 100 epochs, single V100 16GB; hyperparameters k_max,j and d_v per problem; complete data-generation recipes in Appendix A.3 (split-step Fourier on 2^13 mesh for Burgers; 2nd-order FD on 421x421 for Darcy; pseudo-spectral Crank-Nicolson dt=1e-4 on 256x256 for NS). Fixed N=1000/200 (or 10000) train/test split; no random seeds, variance, or error bars reported
quotable_finding: The Fourier neural operator is the first ML-based method to successfully model turbulent flows with zero-shot super-resolution. (Abstract, p.1)
relevance_rqs: RQ1: evidence for fluids/subsurface problem classes and inverse-design loops (airfoil motivating example, Bayesian inverse problems). RQ2: component evidence - Fourier layers, purely data-driven loss with no collocation/residual terms, FFT-based quasi-linear complexity. RQ3: physics enters via solver-generated training data rather than residual penalties - the operator-learning alternative to PINN enforcement mechanisms. RQ4: reliability evidence - resolution invariance, zero-shot super-resolution, no accuracy degradation in downstream MCMC despite speedup
manuscript_section: S4 methods (operator-learning branch and its contrast with PINN enforcement); T1 (architecture/enforcement taxonomy row); S5 fluids paragraph; speedup/efficiency discussion (F-figure on compute trade-offs)
cross_paper_links: builds-on: Li et al. 2020b 'Neural Operator: Graph Kernel Network' (arXiv:2003.03485) - FNO replaces its kernel integral operator with a Fourier-space parameterization; compares-to: DeepONet (PINN-B12, Lu et al. 2019) - cited as prior neural-operator work, and MGNO is described as 'similar to the stacked DeepONet'; contrasts PINN-A01 (Raissi et al. 2019): PINNs 'aim at the latter [solving one PDE instance] and can therefore be computationally expensive... impractical for applications where a solution to the PDE is required for many different instances of the parameter' (p.4); compares-to GNO/MGNO (Li et al. 2020a, Multipole Graph Neural Operator); cites Neural-FEM-style approaches: E & Yu 2018 (Deep Ritz), Bar & Sochen 2019, Smith et al. 2020 (Eikonet), Patel et al. 2021 (physics-informed operator regression); meshfree flow super-resolution context: Jiang et al. 2020 (MeshfreeFlowNet), Kashinath et al. 2021
notes_caveats: Not a PINN - it is the canonical data-driven operator-learning paper; useful in the survey precisely as the counterpoint to residual-based physics enforcement. All benchmarks are synthetic math-benchmarks (no experimental data, no real geometry); Darcy uses fixed forcing f=1 and piecewise-constant coefficients (values 12/3); NS is restricted to the unit torus with fixed forcing, and the headline NS table fixes 64x64 (super-resolution evaluated only on one case, qualitatively). The 'three orders of magnitude faster' claim is inference-time only (training + data generation of 12 hours excluded, though the authors acknowledge this); no seeds/variance reported; Bayesian inverse validation is qualitative (posterior-mean comparison). Table 1 prints FNO-3D parameters as '0.6,558,537' (apparent typo; FNO-2D is 411,517)
